**The Second Coming**  
A 1919 poem famous for the opening line “Turning and turning in the widening gyre” and the apocalyptic image of a “rough beast…slouching towards Bethlehem,” often quoted in cultural references.

**Sailing to Byzantium**  
A 1928 poem in which Yeats imagines escaping the decay of the mortal world for an eternal artistic realm; it contains the line “An aged man is but a paltry thing” and the refrain “tread softly because you tread on my dreams.”

**“An aged man is but a paltry thing”**  
A striking line from “Sailing to Byzantium” that encapsulates Yeats’s view of old age and the desire for artistic transcendence; it is repeatedly cited in discussions of his later work.

**“Things fall apart; the centre cannot hold”**  
The opening line of “The Second Coming,” a widely quoted aphorism used to describe social or political chaos; it introduces the poem’s theme of disintegration.

**“The falcon cannot hear the falconer”**  
A line from “The Second Coming” that symbolizes the loss of control and the breakdown of order; it is a key image that students often remember.

**Spiritus Mundi**  
Latin for “world spirit,” the mythical repository of collective human memory that Yeats invokes in “The Second Coming” to explain the origin of the “rough beast” vision.

**Leda and the Swan**  
A 1923 poem retelling the myth of Zeus’s rape of Leda in swan form; it is a classic example of Yeats’s use of myth to explore themes of power and violence.

**Easter, 1916**  
A poem commemorating the Irish uprising; its refrain “A terrible beauty is born” and its meditation on sacrifice and heroism are central to Yeast’s political poetry.

**The Lake Isle of Innisfree** (or “Innisfree”)  
A lyrical poem in which the speaker longs to escape urban life and build a simple cabin of “clay and wattles” on a tranquil lake; it epitomizes Yeats’s early romantic nature imagery.

**The Wild Swans at Coole**  
A 1917 poem reflecting on aging and the passage of time through the observation of swans; it contains the refrain “the heart of a swan / Has not grown old” and mentions a “vast image out of Spiritus Mundi.”

**The Tower**  
A 1928 collection (and title poem) that marks Yeats’s transition to a more modernist style; the poem “The Tower” includes the line “I have built / My tower for the eyes of men.”  

**Golden Dawn feud with Aleister Crowley**  
A biographical incident in which Yeats physically pushed the occultist Aleister Crowley down the stairs during a dispute within the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn; it illustrates Yeats’s involvement in early 20th‑century esoteric circles.
